topics.title: How Societies Organize Their People
passage: Throughout history, human societies have organized people into different groups and levels, often called a social structure, which determines things like a person's job, rights, and responsibilities within their community. In many ancient civilizations, this structure looked like a pyramid, with a small number of powerful rulers at the top and a much larger number of workers, farmers, or laborers at the bottom.

In some historical societies, a person's position was determined mostly by birth, meaning children generally stayed in the same social level as their parents no matter their individual skills or effort. This kind of rigid structure made it very difficult for someone born into a lower level to move upward, a limitation that shaped nearly every aspect of a person's life, including their education, marriage, and career.

Other societies allowed for slightly more movement between levels, especially for people who gained wealth through trade, skilled craftsmanship, or military service. Merchants and skilled workers in some medieval towns, for example, could sometimes improve their social standing over time, even though the highest positions of power usually remained reserved for a small group of nobles or religious leaders.

Modern societies generally allow far more movement between social and economic levels than in the past, largely because education, career choice, and voting rights are no longer determined solely by a person's family background in most countries. However, sociologists point out that factors like family wealth, access to good schools, and where a person lives can still make it easier or harder for someone to improve their circumstances.

Understanding how societies are structured helps historians and sociologists explain why certain groups had more opportunities than others throughout history, and why some inequalities persist even today. Studying these patterns also helps people evaluate how fair or flexible a particular society's structure truly is, beyond just how it is officially described on paper.

questions.question: What is the main idea of this passage?
options: All societies throughout history have organized people in exactly the same way.
Human societies have organized people into different levels in various ways throughout history, with modern societies generally allowing more movement between levels.
Social structure has no effect on a person's opportunities.
Only ancient civilizations had any kind of social structure.

topics.title: Types of Government Around the World
passage: A government is the system that makes and enforces the rules and laws within a country or region, and different governments organize this power in very different ways. Understanding how a government works helps explain who makes important decisions for a country, how leaders are chosen, and how much say ordinary citizens have in shaping the laws that affect their daily lives.

In a democracy, citizens typically vote to choose their leaders and, in some cases, vote directly on important laws or issues. Most modern democracies are representative, meaning citizens elect representatives who then make decisions and laws on their behalf, rather than every citizen voting on every single law directly, which would be difficult to manage in a large country.

A monarchy, by contrast, places power in the hands of a king, queen, or other royal ruler, often passed down within a single family from one generation to the next. Some monarchies today are absolute, meaning the monarch holds nearly complete power, while others are constitutional, meaning the monarch's power is limited by a constitution and elected officials handle most day-to-day governing decisions.

Other forms of government concentrate power even more tightly, sometimes in a single ruler or a small group with very few limits placed on their authority, and citizens in these systems typically have little or no ability to vote for their leaders or influence major decisions. Historians and political scientists study these different systems to understand how power is gained, used, and sometimes abused throughout history.

Many countries have changed their form of government over time, sometimes gradually and sometimes suddenly, often in response to major events, public demands for change, or shifts in who holds military or economic power. Studying these different government types helps people understand not just how a country is run today, but why its political system developed the way it did.

questions.question: What is the main idea of this passage?
options: Every country in the world uses the exact same type of government.
Countries organize governing power in different ways, ranging from democracies to monarchies to more tightly controlled systems.

topics.title: Why Societies Need Laws and Rules
passage: Every society, no matter how large or small, develops rules to guide how people interact with one another, protect individuals, and keep order within a community. These rules can range from informal customs, like waiting in line, to formal, written laws enforced by courts and government officials, with serious consequences for anyone who breaks them.

Laws serve several important purposes within a society, including protecting people's safety, property, and basic rights, while also creating a shared understanding of what behavior is acceptable. Without agreed-upon laws, resolving disagreements between people would depend entirely on individual strength or personal opinion, rather than a fair, consistent system that applies to everyone.

In most modern societies, laws are created, interpreted, and enforced by three separate parts of government working together. One part creates new laws, another applies and enforces those laws in daily situations, and a third interprets what the laws mean when disagreements or unclear situations arise, particularly in court cases where judges must decide how a law applies to a specific case.

Laws are not fixed forever; they often change over time as a society's values, technology, and challenges evolve. New laws are sometimes created to address problems that did not exist decades earlier, such as rules about internet privacy, while older laws that no longer reflect a society's values may be changed or removed entirely through a formal legal process.

Beyond formal laws, informal social norms, unwritten expectations about polite or appropriate behavior, also help societies function smoothly. While breaking a social norm, like cutting in line, might not lead to legal punishment, it often results in social disapproval, showing that both written laws and unwritten expectations work together to help hold a community together.

questions.question: What is the main idea of this passage?
options: Societies have no need for rules or laws of any kind.
Laws and social norms both play important roles in helping societies function fairly and stay organized.
Laws never change once they are created.

options: New laws are only created to remove old, unnecessary customs.
Society's values, technology, and challenges evolve, creating new problems that need addressing, such as internet privacy.

topics.title: Trade, Money, and Economic Systems
passage: An economic system is the way a society organizes the production, distribution, and use of goods and services, answering basic questions like what to produce, how to produce it, and who gets to use the final products. Every society throughout history, from small farming villages to massive modern nations, has needed some kind of economic system to function.

Long before money existed, many early societies relied on a system called bartering, directly trading one good or service for another without using any kind of currency. Bartering worked reasonably well in small communities, but it created challenges when two people wanted to trade but neither had exactly what the other needed, a problem economists call the "double coincidence of wants."

The invention of money helped solve this problem by giving people a widely accepted way to exchange value without needing to trade goods directly. Early forms of money included items like shells, salt, and precious metals, valued because they were rare, durable, and widely recognized, eventually evolving into the coins and paper currency, and now digital payments, that many societies use today.

Modern economic systems generally fall somewhere between two basic approaches. In a market-based system, individuals and businesses make most decisions about what to produce and sell based on supply and demand, with limited government involvement. In a more centrally planned system, the government plays a much larger role in deciding what gets produced and how resources are distributed among the population.

In reality, most modern countries use a mixed economic system, combining elements of both approaches rather than relying entirely on one or the other. Governments in mixed economies often allow businesses to operate relatively freely while still setting certain rules, providing some public services, and stepping in during economic emergencies to help stabilize the overall system.

questions.question: What is the main idea of this passage?
options: Economic systems have never changed throughout human history.
Societies have developed different economic systems over time, from bartering to money to modern mixed economies.
Bartering is still the primary way most modern countries trade goods.
Money has never played any role in how societies organize trade.

Salt
Precious metals

Decisions are based on supply and demand.
Government involvement is limited.

questions.question: Based on the passage, why did the invention of money help solve problems created by bartering?
options: Money eliminated the need for any trade at all.
Money gave people a widely accepted way to exchange value without needing to trade goods directly.
Money made bartering illegal in most societies.
Money could only be used by governments, not individuals.

questions.question: Which title best fits Paragraph 5?
options: The History of Bartering
How Most Countries Use Mixed Economic Systems
The Invention of Coins and Paper Money
Market-Based Systems Explained

questions.question: In your own words, explain what a "mixed economic system" is, based on the passage.
questions.sample_answer: A mixed economic system combines elements of both market-based and centrally planned systems, allowing businesses to operate freely while the government still sets rules and provides services.
